description: Non-literal meaning — pervasive in ordinary speech, not a poetic extra. Most utterances are not meant literally (metaphor, idiom, metonymy, hyperbole, irony saturate everyday language; cf. Lakoff & Johnson, metaphor is conceptual, not decorative). Comprehending ANY speech requires mapping a literal surface to a non-literal intent. This is the same cross-domain grounding the agent uses elsewhere: a figurative expression maps structure from a source domain onto a target. It is also why the trope NAMES themselves must be read figuratively — 'RedShirt', 'ChekhovsGun', 'TheCoconutEffect' compress a pattern into a metaphor, so grounding the name is itself a figurative-mapping task.

concepts.name: non_literal_meaning
concepts.definition: The general fact that what is said and what is meant diverge — the listener must compute an intended meaning the surface form does not state. The umbrella under which metaphor, idiom, irony, and implicature sit; a comprehension system that takes language literally fails on most of it.

concepts.name: metaphor
concepts.definition: A structured mapping from a source domain onto a target ('time is money', 'the argument collapsed') — understanding borrows inference structure across domains. Conceptual, not ornamental: much abstract thought is comprehended via concrete-domain metaphors. The same cross-domain grounding the agent performs when grounding a concept by analogy.

concepts.name: metonymy
concepts.definition: Naming a thing by something associated with it ('the crown' for monarchy, 'the White House said'). Comprehended by following the standing association from the named stand-in to the intended referent.

concepts.name: idiom
concepts.definition: A fixed expression whose meaning is not composed from its parts ('kick the bucket', 'spill the beans') — a frozen compression that must be grounded as a whole, not parsed. Trope names behave like idioms: the phrase denotes the whole pattern, not its literal words.

concepts.name: hyperbole
concepts.definition: Deliberate overstatement not meant to be taken at face value ('I've told you a million times'). Comprehended by recognising the violation of plausibility as a signal to scale the literal claim down to its intended force.

concepts.name: simile_analogy
concepts.definition: An explicit comparison ('brave as a lion') that licenses transferring selected properties from a vehicle to a tenor. The overt, marked cousin of metaphor; understanding selects WHICH properties the comparison intends.
